questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What privileged-instruction isolation prevents
questions.learningObjective: Identify why a user-mode program cannot execute a privileged instruction
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer wonders why the star-chart viewer on the club laptop cannot stop the CPU's timer directly, even though it runs as an ordinary program.

options.text: Those timer instructions are privileged and only execute while the processor runs in kernel mode.
The viewer is written in a language with no timer support, so no timer instruction is ever generated.
options.misconception: blames a missing language feature rather than the mode bit

options.text: The instructions exist on the chip but only work while the processor runs in real-time mode.
options.misconception: confuses processor execution modes with clock synchronisation

options.text: Modern processors delete every timer instruction so that the chip draws less power.
options.misconception: assumes modern chips remove instructions to save power

questions.explanation: Privileged instructions are gated by the processor's execution mode, so a user-mode program traps into the kernel instead of running them. Language support and power draw are unrelated to that mode check.
questions.hint: Which processor mode makes the instruction legal to run?

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What separating two processes' address spaces buys
questions.learningObjective: Explain what separate address spaces prevent between two programs
questions.stem: A club log records two programs on the imaging laptop: the capture program writes only into its own buffer region, and a second program tries to read that same region directly.

options.text: Each program gets a private copy of every other program's memory, so reads never fail.
options.misconception: believes separate spaces duplicate memory rather than isolating it

options.text: Each program sees only its own mapped memory, and direct reads of the other region fail.
The programs still share one physical memory, and the operating system copies data on every call.
options.misconception: mistakes inter-process copying for address space isolation

options.text: The programs run on different processor cores, so they never read the same memory at once.
options.misconception: assumes address space separation is the same as multicore scheduling

questions.explanation: Separate address spaces give each program its own mapping, so a pointer in one program cannot reach the other's memory. Physical memory may still be shared underneath, which is why the copy-per-call and multicore readings are wrong.
questions.hint: What does a program's pointer actually reach?

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a deny-list instruction policy misses
questions.learningObjective: Explain the coverage gap in a deny-list instruction policy
questions.stem: The observatory's instruction-monitoring experiment records every instruction the imaging program attempts, then blocks only those on a list of twelve known-dangerous instructions.

answer.exemplar: A deny-list blocks only the instructions someone anticipated and wrote down, so a novel or unlisted instruction, including an obscure device-control opcode, still runs freely. It proves nothing about instructions that were never catalogued, so the policy constrains a named set rather than the program's whole capability, and the gap widens as new instructions appear.

questions.explanation: The list enumerates known bad instructions, so anything unlisted passes through unchecked. A deny-list therefore constrains a named set rather than the program's full capability, and the gap grows as new instructions appear.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to an instruction nobody listed.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a bit-for-bit copy preserves that a file copy does not
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a bit-for-bit copy preserves beyond the live files

stimulus.body: From the dome log: copied the club laptop's drive to the archive drive with the imaging software's own copy function, then ran a byte-count check and the file count matched. I did not use a write blocker or clone the raw device, so I assume the copy is equivalent.

questions.stem: The club member reading that log entry wants to correct the assumption it contains. Which statement best explains what a bit-for-bit copy preserves that the software file copy does not?

options.text: The software copy preserves only the directory listing, so empty file bodies are lost when it runs.
options.misconception: believes a file copy keeps only directory metadata

options.text: The software copy keeps modification times but drops the file allocation map entirely.
options.misconception: invented a metadata split with no basis in how copies work

options.text: The software copy handles files it recognises; a bit-for-bit clone captures the whole device, including deleted and unallocated space.
The software copy preserves ownership and permissions, while a bit-for-bit clone discards all filesystem metadata.
options.misconception: reverses the real difference between file and device copies

questions.explanation: A file-level copy moves only the files the tool can enumerate, so deleted and unallocated remnants stay behind on the original. A device-level clone copies every sector, which is why byte counts matching does not make the two equivalent.
questions.hint: What does the copy tool choose to leave behind?

questions.stem: Stage one: a member hashes the acquisition image of a suspect laptop and records the digest. Stage two: the same laptop runs for another hour before imaging, and the image is rehashed. What does the original digest still establish at that later point?

options.text: It establishes that the second image is identical, because a digest describes the device rather than the file.
options.misconception: believes a digest describes hardware instead of a byte sequence

options.text: It establishes that neither image was altered, because a digest cannot be recomputed by hand.
options.misconception: thinks digests are values nobody can recompute

options.text: It establishes that the two images have the same size, since digest length reflects image length.
options.misconception: confuses digest length with the length of the file hashed

options.text: It establishes the integrity of the first image as acquired, and says nothing about the later image.

questions.explanation: A digest is computed from the bytes of the image that was hashed, so it pins that byte sequence only. The later image has different content, and the earlier digest cannot vouch for it.
questions.hint: Which bytes does a digest actually describe?

questions.topic: Why a deleted file can still yield content
questions.learningObjective: Explain why deleted file content can still be recovered
questions.stem: A member deletes a catalogue of star positions from the laptop and replaces nothing, then wonders why a well-equipped examiner might still recover the file's contents.

options.text: Deleting a file usually only marks its space reusable, so the data stays on the medium until overwritten.
The file is copied automatically to the observatory's backup server before every deletion.
options.misconception: assumes every deletion triggers an automatic backup copy

options.text: The operating system encrypts deleted data using a key kept in the file's own metadata.
options.misconception: invents a deletion-time encryption scheme that does not exist

options.text: The laptop keeps a hidden duplicate of every file in a shadow copy that ordinary users can open.
options.misconception: believes shadow copies are readable by any user

questions.explanation: Deletion unlinks the name and releases the blocks rather than erasing them, so the bytes remain readable until something else is written there. Backups, encryption and shadow copies are separate features that the log gives no evidence for.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What volatility argues for in the order of collection
questions.learningObjective: Explain how volatility shapes the order of collection
questions.stem: The club's incident-response note lists a powered-on laptop as the first collection target and a switched-off server as a later one.

answer.exemplar: Data held only in RAM disappears the moment power is lost, so a powered-on machine holds evidence that a switched-off one no longer contains: running processes, open network connections and decrypted keys. Collecting the live system first preserves that volatile evidence, while disk contents survive a shutdown and can safely wait their turn.

questions.explanation: Volatility ranks evidence by how quickly it disappears. Live memory and connection state vanish at power-off, while stored disk data persists, so the decaying evidence is collected first.
questions.hint: Rank the items by how fast the evidence disappears.

questions.topic: What separating two processes' address spaces buys
questions.learningObjective: Interpret memory map evidence about separate address spaces

stimulus.body: Dome log, 23:40: the focus motor routine and the camera utility both run on the club laptop. I dumped both memory maps and noticed the two programs use the same physical pages for their buffers, yet each one's pointer values resolve to different physical addresses.

options.text: The two programs share every page, so a write by one is always immediately visible to the other.
options.misconception: reads shared physical pages as a shared virtual address space

options.text: The programs run in the same address space, because their pointer values resolve to the same addresses.
options.misconception: ignores the translation from virtual to physical addresses

options.text: The programs are separated, but the camera utility can still read the focus routine's buffers directly.
options.misconception: assumes separate spaces still permit direct cross-process reads

options.text: The programs have separate virtual address spaces, and per-process translation hides the shared physical pages.

questions.explanation: Different virtual addresses resolving to different physical pages show two independent mappings, which is what separate address spaces look like. Sharing a physical page underneath is a deliberate mapping, not a breach of the boundary.

options.text: The name pattern still cannot cover unlisted instructions, so the gap that matters is unchanged.
Instruction names are not available when decisions are made, so the extra rule can never be evaluated.
options.misconception: assumes the check has no instruction name to inspect

options.text: The extra rule would block more than half the imaging program's instructions, making it unusable.
options.misconception: judges a rule by how much it blocks rather than what it constrains

options.text: Copying instructions are harmless, so the extra rule only blocks useful imaging operations.
options.misconception: believes copy-type instructions can never matter for safety

questions.explanation: Adding a naming pattern extends a list that was already incomplete, so the class of instructions nobody thought of still runs. The strength of a deny-list is its size, and its weakness is everything it forgot.

questions.topic: What an allow-list instruction policy expresses
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an instruction trace against an allow-list policy
questions.stem: The imaging program's session trace shows 500 attempted instructions: 320 matched the allow-list, 150 were blocked, and 30 were never classified because the tracer lost them.

options.text: The allow-list blocked 30 percent of the program's instructions, and the remaining 30 are unclassified.
options.misconception: reads the unclassified group as automatically harmless

options.text: The tracer classified all 500 instructions, since 320 plus 150 plus 30 covers the whole trace.
options.misconception: adds a losing tracer's count as if it were sound

options.text: The allow-list permitted 320 of the 500 attempts, and 30 attempts escaped classification entirely.
The allow-list permitted 64 percent of the classified instructions, so the trace shows a 64 percent pass rate.
options.misconception: computes a share over a filtered subset and calls it the whole

questions.explanation: The trace's categories are 320 permitted, 150 blocked and 30 unclassified, so the allow-list let through 320 of the 500 attempts. The 64 percent figure uses the wrong denominator, and the unclassified attempts prove nothing about safety.
questions.hint: Check which group the percentage is divided by.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What an image digest establishes and when it stops holding
questions.learningObjective: Explain the scope and the limits of an image digest
questions.stem: A club member asks an examiner to explain the difference between what an image digest proves at the moment of acquisition and what it says about that image an hour later.

answer.exemplar: A digest is computed from the exact bytes of the image at acquisition, so it pins that byte sequence and reveals any later alteration of the same file. It says nothing about the source device afterwards, because the device can be used, changed or wiped without touching the already-acquired image, whose digest still matches its original value.

questions.explanation: The digest pins the byte sequence that was hashed, so it detects changes to that file. The source device can be used or wiped afterwards, which changes nothing about the acquired image and its recorded digest.
questions.hint: Separate the file from the device it came from.

questions.topic: Why a deleted file can still yield content
questions.learningObjective: Explain why emptying the recycle bin does not remove data
questions.stem: A member asks whether emptying the recycle bin on the imaging laptop is enough to make a catalogue file unrecoverable. Which answer is correct?

options.text: No, because the recycle bin only hides the file until the next power cycle of the laptop.
options.misconception: treats the recycle bin as a timed, self-clearing cache

options.text: No, because emptying the bin drops a directory entry and leaves the data on the medium.
Yes, because emptying the bin overwrites the file's clusters with zeros straight away.
options.misconception: believes deletion overwrites the sectors immediately

options.text: Yes, because the file was only copied once and the original copy is untouched.
options.misconception: assumes a copy operation leaves the source file intact

questions.explanation: Emptying the bin removes the directory entry that pointed at the data, leaving the blocks themselves alone until they are reused. Overwriting at deletion time and duplicate copies are behaviours the log gives no support for.
questions.hint: Distinguish removing the name from removing the bytes.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What privileged-instruction isolation prevents
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a trace that records requests for privileged operations

stimulus.body: Dome log: I traced the focus motor program and saw it repeatedly ask the driver to move the axis. Each request produced a trap into the kernel followed by a return, and the program itself never changed the processor's mode on its own.

questions.stem: Given that log entry, what does the tracing show about the imaging program's use of privileged instructions?

options.text: The program executed privileged instructions directly, because the trace recorded the traps as calls.
options.misconception: mistakes a processor trap for direct privileged execution

options.text: The program never touched privileged instructions, because the driver refused every request.
options.misconception: confuses refused requests with instructions that were absent

options.text: The program requested privileged operations and the kernel performed them in a more privileged mode.
The program and the kernel shared one address space, so the traps were ordinary function calls.
options.misconception: assumes a trap is just a function call in one space

questions.explanation: A trap into the kernel and a return shows the program requesting a privileged action that the kernel carried out in its own mode. Direct execution, refusal and shared-space function calls contradict that sequence.
questions.hint: A trap is a handover, not an execution.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What separating two processes' address spaces buys
questions.learningObjective: Explain the investigative value of address space isolation
questions.stem: A member asks an examiner what isolation between two programs' address spaces buys when one of those programs is suspected of having run malicious code.

answer.exemplar: Separate address spaces mean the suspect program cannot name or overwrite another program's memory, because its pointers resolve only within its own mapping and cross-process reads fail unless a region is explicitly shared. A malicious process is therefore contained, so damage stops at the boundary the designer drew instead of reaching every other program on the machine.

questions.explanation: Isolation confines a malicious program to its own mapping, so it cannot read or corrupt another program's memory directly. That containment is what limits the blast radius and gives an examiner a defensible picture of what was and was not reachable.
questions.hint: Ask where the malicious program's pointers can land.

questions.learningObjective: Assess deny-list coverage using instruction counts
questions.stem: Over a month the club's imaging program used 340 distinct instructions, and the deny-list names 12 of them, of which 4 never actually appear. A scanned sample executed 9 instructions, none of which is on the list.

options.text: The deny-list stops the sample, because the sample draws its instructions from the same 340.
options.misconception: assumes any program uses only the known instruction set

options.text: The deny-list stops the sample's 9 instructions, because 12 listed entries exceed 9 attempts.
options.misconception: treats the length of the list as if it were coverage

options.text: The deny-list blocks nothing in the sample, but it would block 8 of the imaging program's 340.
options.misconception: miscounts the instructions the imaging program actually uses

options.text: The deny-list stops none of the sample's 9 instructions, because none of them appears on the list.

questions.explanation: Blocking depends on membership of the list, and none of the sample's nine instructions is on it, so nothing is blocked. List length says nothing about coverage of instructions a program might choose.
questions.hint: Blocking is decided by list membership alone.

A file-level copy of the user's home directory, because it preserves the files that matter most.
options.misconception: believes the relevant evidence is only the live user files

options.misconception: treats compression as a lossless forensic acquisition

options.text: A live screen capture of the running system, because what is displayed is the true state.

questions.topic: What an image digest establishes and when it stops holding
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a digest that no longer matches the image
questions.stem: Stage one: an examiner hashes the image and the digest matches the value recorded in the club's evidence log. Stage two: the examiner opens the image and finds one sector's bytes were edited after the digest was taken.

options.text: The digest proves the image was altered, so the examiner must discard the whole acquisition.
options.misconception: confuses a stale digest with proof of tampering

options.text: The digest pinned the image as acquired, and the later edit breaks that match in a detectable way.
The digest proves the acquisition was valid, so the later edit is beside the point.
options.misconception: assumes an earlier matching digest covers later edits

options.text: The digest proves the examiner made the edit while imaging the device.
options.misconception: assigns the edit to imaging without any evidence

questions.explanation: The recorded digest describes the bytes present at acquisition, so a later edit makes the recomputed digest disagree and reveals the change. It does not identify who made the edit, and a mismatch is not proof that the acquisition was bad.
questions.hint: Compare what the digest was taken over and when.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a deleted file can still yield content
questions.learningObjective: Explain how deleted data survives on a magnetic disk
questions.stem: A member asks how a deleted file can still be recovered from a magnetic disk even though the file's directory entry is gone.

answer.exemplar: Deleting a file unlinks its name and marks the blocks free, but the bytes stay in those blocks until something else is written there. Recovery therefore reads the raw device looking for the old content, which may still sit in unallocated space or in the tail of a partly reused file, provided none of it has been overwritten.

questions.explanation: Unlinking frees the blocks rather than clearing them, so the bytes linger in unallocated space or in the slack of a reused file. Recovery works because the content is still there until a later write replaces it.
questions.hint: Where do the bytes live after the name is removed?

answer.exemplar: Privileged instructions may execute only while the processor runs in a more privileged mode. options.text: The two programs share one address space, because both refer to virtual page 0x4000.
options.misconception: treats equal virtual addresses as a shared address space

options.text: The programs have separate address spaces, and sharing a physical page is an explicit mapping choice.
The mapping table is corrupt, because a physical page cannot be mapped twice.
options.misconception: assumes a physical page may map into only one space

options.text: The programs run in kernel mode, because user-mode programs cannot map physical pages.
options.misconception: infers a privilege level from a mapping table entry

questions.explanation: The same virtual page resolving to different physical pages proves two independent mappings, and a shared physical page is a deliberate arrangement rather than a fault. Nothing in the mapping entries implies corruption or kernel mode.
questions.hint: Read the translation, not the virtual address.

options.misconception: reduces the difference to checking cost rather than coverage

options.text: Both policies block the same instructions in practice, because real instruction lists are complete.
options.misconception: assumes real instruction lists are exhaustive

options.text: An allow-list is weaker because it applies only to whole programs and not to individual instructions.
options.misconception: believes instruction allow-lists work at program granularity

options.text: A deny-list's weakness is that unlisted instructions still run, whatever their effect on legitimate work.

questions.explanation: The deny-list problem is coverage, not collateral damage: instructions nobody listed keep running. An allow-list reverses the default so that unknown instructions are refused, which is what the debate should have compared.

questions.stem: The imaging program's instruction allow-list covers 55 percent of the instructions it attempts, and one session contains 1,200 attempted instructions. How many of the attempted instructions are denied in that session?
questions.explanation: The denied share is 100 minus 55 percent, which is 45 percent, and 45 percent of 1,200 is 540 instructions. Applying 55 percent to the total would count the permitted instructions instead.

options.text: The checksum match proves the copy is identical, so the file-level approach is equivalent.
options.misconception: assumes one matching checksum generalises to the whole image

questions.explanation: Checksums and byte counts describe the files that were copied, and a file-level tool never touches deleted or unallocated space. A match on those measures says nothing about the regions the copy skipped.

options.misconception: believes clock drift destroys file content

questions.topic: What separating two processes' address spaces buys
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of address space isolation
questions.stem: A member observes that two programs in separate address spaces can still interfere with each other and asks how that is possible.

answer.exemplar: Isolation blocks direct reads and writes across the boundary, but channels such as shared files, pipes, sockets and shared memory still carry data between the two, and a program may also misconfigure a buffer it does own. questions.explanation: Address spaces block direct memory access between programs, not the data paths they share deliberately. Shared files, pipes and sockets remain, so isolation narrows the damage rather than ruling it out.

questions.explanation: The monitor checked 214 instructions but blocked only 6, so the great majority were observed and allowed to run. Checking an instruction is not the same as denying it, and six blocks did not stop the sample.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a deleted file can still yield content
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a free-space wipe affects recoverability
questions.stem: A member runs a file-wiping tool that claims to overwrite free space on the imaging laptop and asks an examiner what that will do to the file deleted last week.

answer.exemplar: A wipe that overwrites free space destroys the blocks that still held the deleted file's bytes, so the content can no longer be recovered even though the directory entry went first. Any wipe that skips unallocated space, or writes only to blocks already reallocated, leaves recoverable remnants behind, so the tool's actual coverage matters more than its presence.

questions.explanation: Free-space overwriting removes the old bytes from the blocks the deleted file occupied, closing the recovery path. A wipe that skips unallocated space or only touches reallocated blocks leaves the content recoverable.
questions.hint: Ask which blocks the tool actually writes to.

questions.explanation: Volatility is a decay measure, so the rule is to collect whatever disappears soonest before it disappears. Capacity, user count and device age say nothing about how quickly evidence is lost.

options.text: Because the interface lets a user program execute privileged instructions directly.

answer.exemplar: A bit-for-bit copy transfers the device's raw sectors, so it preserves everything the medium holds: deleted files, slack space inside partly used clusters, and data sitting outside any filesystem. questions.stem: A triage table lists item A as network-attached storage where power state is irrelevant, item B as a laptop with battery charge and an open session marked for collection today, and item C as a desktop tower powered down since the incident marked for collection this week.

options.text: Item A is the most volatile because network-attached storage is always live.
options.misconception: calls remote storage volatile without evidence

options.text: Item B is urgent only because its battery would otherwise die during the week.
options.misconception: reduces the urgency to a battery-charge problem

options.text: Item C is last because desktops hold less data than laptops do.
options.misconception: ranks by expected data volume

options.text: Item B is urgent because its running state decays, while the other two hold stored data.

questions.explanation: Item B's open session holds state that power loss would erase, so the table's schedule follows decay rates. Battery life, data volume and the live status of remote storage do not explain the ordering given.
questions.hint: Ask what each item would lose if it were switched off.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What privileged-instruction isolation prevents
questions.learningObjective: State what makes an instruction privileged and where it is checked
questions.stem: A new club member asks the examiner to state what makes an instruction privileged and where that condition is enforced.

answer.exemplar: An instruction is privileged when the processor will only execute it while running in a more privileged mode, normally the kernel's mode. The check is carried out by the processor itself as it decodes the instruction, so a program in a less privileged mode cannot execute it directly and instead traps to the kernel for help.

questions.explanation: Privilege is a property of the instruction combined with the current processor mode, and the processor enforces it at decode time. The kernel is not consulted first, so the enforcement point is the hardware itself.
questions.hint: Recall where the mode is checked during decoding.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What separating two processes' address spaces buys
questions.learningObjective: Identify a practical consequence of separate address spaces
questions.stem: Which of these is a practical consequence of giving each program its own address space?

options.text: Each program gets its own copy of every shared library that it loads.
options.misconception: believes separate spaces duplicate shared library code

options.text: Programs can no longer use shared files or sockets to exchange information.
options.misconception: assumes address spaces remove every inter-process channel

options.text: A bug in one program is less likely to corrupt another program's memory by accident.
Every program must now be loaded at the same virtual addresses on every machine.
options.misconception: confuses per-process mapping with a fixed system-wide layout

questions.explanation: Per-process mappings mean a stray write lands in the offending program's own space, so accidental corruption of a neighbour is much less likely. Libraries are still shared, channels such as sockets remain, and loading addresses are chosen per process.
questions.hint: Think about where a bad pointer lands.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a deny-list instruction policy misses
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a longer deny-list still leaves a coverage gap
questions.stem: A club member observes that the deny-list grew from twelve entries to forty entries and asks why the policy is still not safe to rely on.

answer.exemplar: Each added entry removes one known instruction from the unknown set, but the set of instructions a program can attempt is far larger than any list anybody has drawn up. The gap persists because the list grows one named case at a time while the space of possible instructions grows on its own, so only a default-deny allow-list can bound what the program may do.

questions.explanation: A longer list closes one known hole at a time while the space of possible instructions keeps expanding, so the unlisted set stays large. Only reversing the default with an allow-list bounds the program's behaviour by construction.
questions.hint: Compare how fast the list grows with how fast the instruction space grows.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What an allow-list instruction policy expresses
questions.learningObjective: Describe an allow-list instruction policy accurately
questions.stem: Which description of an allow-list instruction policy is accurate?

options.text: It blocks the instructions on a published list of known-dangerous operations.
options.misconception: describes a deny-list while naming an allow-list

options.text: It records every instruction that was used so the behaviour can be reviewed later.
options.misconception: describes logging rather than enforcement

options.text: It permits the listed instructions and lets the rest run under a warning.
options.misconception: turns enforcement into a warning-only advisory

options.text: It permits only the listed instructions and refuses everything else by default.

questions.explanation: An allow-list states membership as permission and absence as refusal, which is why it bounds behaviour without needing to anticipate every danger. Blocking a known-danger list and recording usage are different mechanisms entirely.
questions.hint: Focus on the default for instructions that are not listed.
